Sudah lama saya mengenal beberapa sisi toba seperti tomok, simar jarunjung, taman simalem, parapat, dan tiga ras namun ada beberapa titik yang belum pernah saya datangi seperti bukit hutaginjang yang terletak di kawasan wisata balige-silangit, beberapa kawasan di timur seperti tongging, paropo silalahi, tele, dan bukit holbung.
 
 Bulan juni 2025 lalu saya sempatkan mampir kesitu dalam perjalanan pulang dari medan ke pekanbaru dengan sengaja memilih rute balige-tarutung-sipirok-gn tua-kota pinang-tol dumai.
 setelah mengikuti gmap dari balige-silangit sampailah saya ditujuan.
 Akses jalan nya bagus ber aspal dan masih terawat, di bukit tersebut dari hp saya menunjukkan berada di posisi ketinggian 1640mdpl yang kabarnya adalah kampung tertinggi di toba dan mungkin tempat tertinggi di toba.
 Seperti kita ketahui bahwa posisi danau toba ada di ketinggian 900mdpl (meter diatas permukaaan laut) dan kedalaman air terdalam caldera (cekungan beentuk kuali) danau toba ini adalah 505m.
 Itu artinya di bukit hutaginjang ini kita melihat kebawah sejauh 740m dimana muka air danau toba dan perkampungan berada dibawah situ sehingga bisa dibayangkan keindahan mata memandang.
 
 Pemandangan nya indah luar biasa dimana kita dapat melihat hamparan pulau samosir bagian selatan daerah Nainggolan dan Onan Runggu.
 Di puncak ini sengaja di datarkan untuk membuat kawasan fasilitas umum seperti:
 -bangunan pendopo dan stage untuk acara
 -warung-warung umkm yang dibangunkan tertata dengan nama menggunakan marga batak seperti warung Siregar, dan seterus nya...
 -toilet yang bersih dan sumber air yang bersih pula
 -sarana paralayang seharga Rp50000 untuk sekali turun melayang (by request)
 -menara kecil view point
 -lahan parkir yang bisa digunakan untuk camping ground saat malam hari.
 -fotografer yang ramah menawarkan jasa nya, sayang saja telescope mereka lagi tidak tersedia saat itu.
 -tersedia penerangan dan sinyal komunikasi disini.
 
 Sayang nya saya tidak sempat menikmati suasana pagi dan malam hari yang tentunya amat dingin. Saya berharap suatu waktu dengan teman-teman atau rombongan keluarga bisa datang kembali kesini untuk ber camping bersama.
 Di warung-warung umkm tersedia yang khusus tentunya kopi tubruk sidikalang dan lintong yang nikmat dengan harga yang sangat terjangkau.
 Semua warung umkm tutup pada malam hari sehingga bagi yang berniat untuk camping haruslah sudah mempersiapkan bekal.
 
 Itulah sekilas kesan saya, dengan harapan agar masyarakat yang berusaha disini selalu memelihara kebersihan dan bila perlu mengedukasi pengunjung untuk ikut bersama menjaga kebersihan, sehingga jawasan ini bisa ikut mengangkat ekonomi masyarakat sekitar, karena kunci minat wisata salah satu nya adalah fasilitas yang lengkap dan bersih serta harga yang wajar.

Followed Google Maps like a loyal adventurer, hoping to stumble upon the famous Batu Marhosa—the mysterious stone said to whistle when the wind hits just right. The location pinned? Yes, we arrived. The vibe? A little more “Where’s the batu?” than “marhosa!”

To be fair, nature was doing its thing—there were signs of recent changes in the area: uprooted trees, shifts in vegetation, and an overall feeling that the landscape had been rearranged by something (weather? time? overzealous goats?). There was a small stream trickling through, sort of a waterfall if you squint, just like a fellow review had described. Peaceful? Yes. Whistling rocks? Not so much.

We poked around a bit, hoping to hear the wind sing through a stone, but it didn’t feel like the kind of place you’d want to start ripping off leaves. More like a spot you pause, take a breath, and then quietly ask Google if maybe the pin’s a little off.

So is it the real Batu Marhosa site? Could be. Is it worth the detour? Only if you’re already in Pangururan and feeling curious, cautious, and equipped with a local guided guide.

Batu Marhosa might not have whistled for us, but the adventure lives on—just a little further up the trail.

Note: If you’re feeling brave, stubborn, and have a heart of steel (and a sturdy bike)—you could venture even further up to Danau Aek Natonang. It’s a crater lake that takes some effort and determination to reach, especially on two wheels. Think gravel, slopes, landslides and a workout for your soul. It’d easily earn you a badge of Samosir explorer pride, and a slice of unknown peace but also magically transported into a near no-mans world that only the locals know

Lake Sidihoni is the kind of place that makes geography teachers giddy. Nestled on Samosir Island, which itself floats in the vast expanse of Lake Toba, Sidihoni earns its quirky nickname: “the lake above the lake.” It’s like nature’s own Russian nesting doll, but with more cows and fewer instructions.

The journey there is an adventure in itself. Expect a bumpy ride especially when we were on 2 wheeler 150cc. Tests your vehicle’s suspension and your patience. But once you arrive, the serene landscape of rolling green hills and tranquil waters offers a peaceful respite. The lake’s surface occasionally changes color, adding a touch of magic to the already picturesque setting.

Facilities are minimal, so come prepared. There’s no entrance fee, but also no restrooms or snack bars. It’s just you, the lake, and perhaps a curious buffalo or two.

A unique geographical gem that rewards the adventurous traveler with its tranquil beauty.

Desa Wisata Tomok Parsaoran is like stepping into a Batak time capsule, but with souvenir stalls. It’s where ancient traditions meet modern bargaining skills, and where you can learn about centuries of culture right before haggling over fridge magnets shaped like buffalo horns.

The village is full of charm, traditional houses with dramatic rooftops, locals who smile like they know something you don’t, and enough carved wooden figures to populate a small army. Wandered into the Batak Museum in Tomok expecting the usual museum vibe… but nope, it was completely unmanned when we arrived—zero staff, zero lights. It felt like we had unlocked a bonus level of Night at the Museum: Batak Edition. Cue us creeping around with a mini torch, hunting for light switches like modern-day explorers. (found them, and yes, we felt like heroes.)

Once lit, the place came alive. Housed in a beautifully preserved Rumah Bolon (traditional Batak longhouse), the museum showcases a fascinating collection of Batak artifacts—from ulos cloths and weapons to carvings with rich symbolic meaning. Every corner whispers stories of Batak life, rituals, and royal legacy but was short of descriptions and had to be dugged up from the www.

Bonus history hit: Tomok is home to the Sidabutar royal tombs, so you’re literally walking through centuries of cultural richness.

Note:
•	Don’t be surprised by the many vendors who would spring at the entrance, surrounding the village are mostly descendants of the Sidabutar family
•	Bring a flashlight or phone torch just in case you end up like us on a cloudy gloomy day that adds to the spook
•	Pair it with a visit to the King Sidabutar Tomb and Sigale-gale performance.
•	Look up the meaning of Batak carvings before you go—it makes everything more meaningful.

Batak Museum Tomok is where history stares at you with carved wooden eyes and centuries of side-eye. Housed in a small traditional Batak house that looks like it could either shelter ancestors or star in a gothic fairytale, this museum packs a lot of cultural soul into one sharp-roofed structure.

Inside, you’ll find ancient artifacts, traditional textiles, and enough statues to make you wonder if one of them might blink. It’s educational, sure, but also the kind of place where the silence feels just a little too respectful.

The best part? You’ll walk out knowing more about Batak customs, architecture, and funerary practices, plus, you’ll finally understand why the buffalo horns on the roof are absolutely not for decoration.

Come for the culture, stay for the ancestral energy, and leave with a healthy respect for anyone carved out of wood.
